explanation: Scarcity means that resources are limited relative to unlimited human wants. It is the fundamental economic problem.
choice0: Limited resources relative to unlimited wants
choice1: An abundance of goods and services
choice2: The study of how governments set prices
choice3: When supply exceeds demand

description: What does the law of demand state?
explanation: The law of demand states that as the price of a good rises the quantity demanded falls all else equal.
choice0: Higher prices lead to higher quantity demanded
choice1: Higher prices lead to lower quantity demanded
choice2: Lower prices lead to lower quantity demanded
choice3: Supply and demand always balance

description: What does the law of supply state?
explanation: The law of supply states that as price rises producers are willing to supply more of a good all else equal.
choice0: Higher prices lead to lower quantity supplied
choice1: Higher prices have no effect on supply
choice2: Higher prices lead to higher quantity supplied
choice3: Lower prices lead to higher quantity supplied

explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up when making a choice.
choice0: The value of the best foregone alternative
choice1: The monetary price paid for a good
choice2: The total cost of all alternatives
choice3: The time spent making a decision

explanation: GDP stands for Gross Domestic Product. It measures the total value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year.
choice0: General Domestic Price
choice1: Gross Demand Product
choice2: Government Debt Policy
choice3: Gross Domestic Product

explanation: Inflation is a general rise in the overall price level in an economy over time reducing the purchasing power of money.
choice0: A fall in the price of one specific good
choice1: A sustained rise in the overall price level
choice2: An increase in real wages
choice3: A decrease in government spending

description: What is a market in economics?
explanation: In economics a market is any arrangement through which buyers and sellers exchange goods services or resources.
choice0: Only a physical place where trading occurs
choice1: Only an online platform for shopping
choice2: Any arrangement where buyers and sellers exchange goods
choice3: A government price-setting committee

explanation: Fiscal policy refers to the use of government spending and taxation to influence the economy.
choice0: Government use of spending and taxes to influence the economy
choice1: Central bank control of the money supply
choice2: A firm's pricing strategy
choice3: Rules regulating international trade

description: What institution typically conducts monetary policy in the United States?
explanation: The Federal Reserve (the Fed) is the central bank of the United States and is responsible for conducting monetary policy.
choice0: The Department of the Treasury
choice1: The Internal Revenue Service
choice2: The President's Council of Economic Advisers
choice3: The Federal Reserve

explanation: Comparative advantage is the ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
choice0: Producing more of every good than competitors
choice1: Producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than others
choice2: Having the most advanced technology
choice3: Having the largest workforce

explanation: A demand curve shows the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity consumers are willing to buy holding other factors constant.
choice0: A curve showing how supply changes with income
choice1: A curve showing government price controls
choice2: A curve showing price versus quantity demanded
choice3: A curve showing total revenue for a firm

explanation: Microeconomics studies the behavior of individual consumers firms and markets rather than the economy as a whole.
choice0: Individual consumers firms and specific markets
choice1: The total output of a national economy
choice2: International trade flows between countries
choice3: Government budget policies

explanation: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole including total output employment and price levels.
choice0: The pricing decisions of a single firm
choice1: Consumer choices in a single market
choice2: The cost structure of individual industries
choice3: The economy as a whole including GDP and inflation

explanation: An export is a good or service produced domestically and sold to buyers in other countries.
choice0: A good bought from another country
choice1: A good sold to another country
choice2: A tax on foreign goods
choice3: A quota on domestic production

description: What happens to a supply curve when production costs rise?
explanation: When production costs rise producers supply less at every price shifting the supply curve to the left.
choice0: The supply curve shifts right
choice1: The demand curve shifts left
choice2: The supply curve shifts left
choice3: The demand curve shifts right

description: If you spend 2 hours studying instead of working a job that pays $10 per hour what is your opportunity cost of studying?
explanation: The opportunity cost is the value of the best foregone alternative. You gave up $20 in wages so that is your opportunity cost.
choice0: $20 in forgone wages
choice1: The cost of your textbooks
choice2: Your tuition fee
choice3: Zero because studying is free

description: Which of the following is NOT counted in GDP?
explanation: GDP counts final goods and services. Intermediate goods used in production are not counted separately to avoid double counting.
choice0: New cars sold to consumers
choice1: Haircuts purchased by households
choice2: Newly built houses sold
choice3: Steel used to make cars (intermediate good)

description: What does a Consumer Price Index (CPI) measure?
explanation: The CPI measures the average change over time in prices paid by consumers for a basket of goods and services.
choice0: The total output of an economy
choice1: The average price level paid by consumers for a basket of goods
choice2: The price of goods traded internationally
choice3: The wages paid to workers

description: How many sellers exist in a perfectly competitive market?
explanation: A perfectly competitive market has many sellers each selling identical products and no single seller can influence the market price.
choice0: One dominant seller
choice1: A small number of large sellers
choice2: Many sellers of identical products
choice3: Two sellers competing for customers

description: Which of the following is an example of fiscal policy?
explanation: Fiscal policy involves government spending and taxation decisions. Cutting income taxes is an example.
choice0: The government cuts income taxes
choice1: The central bank raises interest rates
choice2: A firm lowers its prices
choice3: Consumers increase their savings

description: What is the primary tool the Federal Reserve uses to influence short-term interest rates?
explanation: The Federal Reserve's primary tool is the federal funds rate - the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans.
choice0: Setting income tax rates
choice1: Changing government spending levels
choice2: Printing physical currency
choice3: Setting the federal funds rate

explanation: The equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded - markets tend to move toward this price.
choice0: The highest price a firm can charge
choice1: The price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded
choice2: The lowest price consumers are willing to pay
choice3: The government-mandated price

description: What does price elasticity of demand measure?
explanation: Price elasticity of demand measures how responsive the quantity demanded is to a change in price.
choice0: How quickly prices change in a market
choice1: How much supply responds to an income change
choice2: How responsive quantity demanded is to a price change
choice3: How sensitive government revenue is to tax changes

explanation: An import is a good or service produced in another country and purchased domestically.
choice0: A good brought in from another country
choice1: A good sold abroad
choice2: A restriction on foreign products
choice3: A domestic subsidy for local producers

explanation: Utility is the satisfaction or benefit a consumer receives from consuming a good or service.
choice0: The physical usefulness of a tool
choice1: The cost of producing a product
choice2: A measure of a firm's profits
choice3: The satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming a good

explanation: A fixed cost is a cost that does not change with the level of output such as rent or insurance premiums.
choice0: A cost that rises with each unit produced
choice1: A cost that does not change with output level
choice2: The cost of raw materials per unit
choice3: A cost set by the government

explanation: A negative externality is a cost imposed on a third party who is not part of a transaction such as pollution from a factory.
choice0: A benefit received by a non-market party
choice1: A loss suffered only by the seller
choice2: A cost imposed on third parties not in the transaction
choice3: A tax imposed by the government

description: If demand for a product increases and supply stays the same what happens to the equilibrium price?
explanation: When demand increases with supply unchanged buyers compete for the same quantity pushing the price up.
choice0: The equilibrium price rises
choice1: The equilibrium price falls
choice2: The equilibrium price stays the same
choice3: The equilibrium quantity falls

description: Which of the following contributes to GDP?
explanation: GDP is measured as C + I + G + (X - M). Consumer spending (C) is the largest component.
choice0: A homeowner cleaning her own house
choice1: Buying a used car from a neighbor
choice2: Underground (illegal) economic activity
choice3: A new smartphone purchased by a consumer

explanation: Deflation is a sustained decrease in the overall price level in an economy.
choice0: A rapid increase in prices
choice1: A sustained decrease in the overall price level
choice2: A one-time price drop in a single market
choice3: An increase in the purchasing power of foreign currency

explanation: A monopoly is a market structure with only one seller who faces no close competition and can influence the market price.
choice0: A market with two equally powerful firms
choice1: A market with many small competing firms
choice2: A market with a single seller who dominates
choice3: A government-run public service

explanation: A tariff is a tax imposed by a government on imported goods raising their price to protect domestic producers.
choice0: A tax on imported goods
choice1: A limit on the quantity of imports
choice2: A government subsidy for exporters
choice3: A free trade agreement between nations

description: What is the term for a choice that gives up the highest-valued alternative?
explanation: The best alternative given up is called the opportunity cost. It is the core of economic decision making.
choice0: Absolute advantage
choice1: Comparative advantage
choice2: Diminishing returns
choice3: Opportunity cost

description: What does the term ceteris paribus mean in economics?
explanation: Ceteris paribus is a Latin phrase meaning all other things being equal. It is used to isolate the effect of one variable.
choice0: Supply equals demand
choice1: All other things being equal
choice2: Prices rise over time
choice3: Goods are scarce

explanation: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price that can be charged for a good. If set below equilibrium it causes a shortage.
choice0: A minimum price set by the government
choice1: The price at which supply equals demand
choice2: A legal maximum price for a good
choice3: The highest price a firm has ever charged

description: Which of the following is a macroeconomic indicator?
explanation: Unemployment rate is a macroeconomic indicator measuring the share of the labor force that is jobless and actively seeking work.
choice0: The national unemployment rate
choice1: The price of one firm's stock
choice2: The wage paid at a single factory
choice3: The cost of producing one car

description: What is a government budget deficit?
explanation: A budget deficit occurs when a government spends more than it collects in tax revenue in a given period.
choice0: When tax revenue exceeds government spending
choice1: When exports exceed imports
choice2: When inflation is above 2%
choice3: When government spending exceeds tax revenue

description: What happens to borrowing when interest rates fall?
explanation: Lower interest rates reduce the cost of borrowing encouraging businesses and consumers to take out more loans.
choice0: Borrowing becomes more expensive
choice1: Borrowing becomes cheaper and tends to increase
choice2: Borrowing stays the same
choice3: Savings rates rise sharply

explanation: A substitute good can replace another good in consumption. If the price of one rises consumers switch to the substitute.
choice0: A good that is consumed alongside another good
choice1: A good that is inferior to another
choice2: A good that can replace another in consumption
choice3: A good with perfectly inelastic demand

description: If a good has inelastic demand a price increase will lead to what change in total revenue?
explanation: With inelastic demand quantity falls less than price rises so total revenue increases when price rises.
choice0: Total revenue increases
choice1: Total revenue decreases
choice2: Total revenue stays the same
choice3: Quantity demanded increases

description: What does the expenditure approach to GDP sum up?
explanation: The expenditure approach adds C (consumption) + I (investment) + G (government spending) + NX (net exports).
choice0: All wages paid to workers in the economy
choice1: All firms' profits in the economy
choice2: All taxes collected by the government
choice3: Consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports

description: What is the term for a very rapid and out-of-control inflation?
explanation: Hyperinflation refers to extremely rapid inflation often seen when governments print large amounts of money.
choice0: Stagflation
choice1: Hyperinflation
choice2: Deflation
choice3: Disinflation

explanation: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a small number of large firms each of which is large enough to influence market prices.
choice0: A market with only one seller
choice1: A market with many small competing sellers
choice2: A market dominated by a few large firms
choice3: A market with free entry and exit

description: What does it mean to have an absolute advantage?
explanation: Absolute advantage means being able to produce more of a good with the same resources compared to another producer.
choice0: Producing a good with greater output per unit of resource
choice1: Producing at a lower opportunity cost
choice2: Exporting more than you import
choice3: Having the lowest prices in a market

explanation: A normal good is one for which demand increases when consumer income increases.
choice0: A good with perfectly elastic demand
choice1: A good with many substitutes
choice2: A good that is always affordable
choice3: A good whose demand rises when income rises

explanation: Marginal cost is the additional cost of producing one more unit of a good.
choice0: The average cost across all units produced
choice1: The extra cost of producing one more unit
choice2: The fixed cost divided by quantity
choice3: The cost of the most expensive input

description: What is an example of a positive externality?
explanation: A positive externality is a benefit received by third parties not involved in a transaction. Education benefits society broadly.
choice0: A factory polluting a nearby river
choice1: A car producing exhaust fumes
choice2: A person getting vaccinated protecting others
choice3: A firm underpaying its workers

explanation: Complement goods are consumed together. When the price of one rises demand for its complement falls.
choice0: A good consumed together with another good such as cars and gasoline
choice1: A good that can replace another good
choice2: A good with very elastic demand
choice3: A good produced by a monopolist

explanation: The unemployment rate is the percentage of people in the labor force who are actively looking for work but do not have a job.
choice0: The share of all adults who do not have a job
choice1: The number of job vacancies in the economy
choice2: The percentage of workers who are part-time
choice3: The percentage of the labor force that is jobless and actively seeking work

explanation: Free trade is an economic policy under which governments impose no restrictions on imports or exports between countries.
choice0: Trade only between neighboring countries
choice1: Trade without government-imposed restrictions
choice2: Trade subsidized by the government
choice3: A policy of maximizing exports and minimizing imports
